# @mission-platform/vite-plugin-jsx

A **two-stage compiler** that turns the framework-neutral components authored
against `@mission-platform/jsx` into **fully native** React or Vue 3 components
at **build time** — with no runtime adapter and no shared "neutral runtime" in
the shipped output.

## Why two stages

`@mission-platform/jsx` lets a component be authored once in classic JSX (the
`h` factory) using React-style hooks (`useState`/`useRef`/`useEffect`/…). To
ship it to a framework *without compromising that framework's runtime
performance*, the compilation is split:

1. **Stage 1 — source-to-source.** The neutral `.tsx` module is parsed with the
   TypeScript compiler API and re-emitted as a per-framework **source module**:
   - **React** → a `.tsx` module: the `@mission-platform/jsx` import is split
     into a value import from `react` (`h` → `createElement`, plus `Fragment`
     and the hooks, which *are* React's own) and a type-only import kept against
     the neutral package; host `class` → `className` and `for` → `htmlFor`.
   - **Vue** → a real `.vue` single-file component (`<script setup lang="tsx">`):
     `defineOptions({ name, inheritAttrs: false })` + `defineProps(…)` (props with
     their defaults). Because `inheritAttrs: false` also disables Vue's *automatic*
     root attribute inheritance, the component's root re-opts back in explicitly
     with `v-bind="$attrs"` (see both emit paths below), so consumer-supplied
     fall-through attributes (`class`/`style`/`id`/`data-*`/listeners) still reach
     the host — matching the hand-authored SFCs these replaced. The React-style
     hooks are translated to Vue
     reactivity/lifecycle (`useState` → `ref`, `useRef` → `ref` + `.current` →
     `.value`, `useMemo` → `computed`, `useEffect` → `onMounted` + `watch(deps)`
     + cleanup on re-run/unmount) emitted **once** at the top level. The returned
     markup is emitted one of two ways:
     - **Native `<template>` (preferred).** Components whose body is a flat list
       of **scalar** derived consts plus a single return have that return's
       JSX/`h()` tree rewritten into real Vue `<template>` markup: a dynamic
       `h(tag, …)`/JSX tag → `<component :is="tag">`; `class`/`style`/`on<Event>`
       (→ `@event`)/`ref`/other dynamic attributes → the matching binding;
       a multi-word `on<Event>` on a **native** element has its event part
       lowercased (`onDragOver` → `@dragover`) so Vue's hyphenation binds the
       real all-lowercase DOM event instead of the dead `drag-over`; listeners on
       **component** elements keep their camelCase form to match the child's emits;
       `cond ? <a/> : <b/>` (or `cond && <a/>`) → `v-if`/`v-else`; and each derived
       scalar const is lifted to a reactive `computed` (the template auto-unwraps
       it). `properties.children`, the normalised child-list spread, and `<Slot>`
       markers → native `<slot>`. A **single** root element is emitted with a
       trailing `v-bind="$attrs"` (placed last to mirror default-inheritance
       precedence; `class`/`style` still merge); a `<Slot>`/fragment/conditional
       root has no single host to bind and is left untouched.
     - **Render-closure fallback.** Bodies outside that shape — node-valued local
       consts, `.map()`/`.flatMap()` lists, prop spreads, or an `MpChild`-typed
       prop rendered as a child (the complex layout components: `BaseTable`,
       `BaseDrawer`, `BaseList`, `BaseHero`, `BaseNavbar`, `BaseVerticalLayout`,
       `BaseWindowPopout`, `BaseApplicationLayout`, `BaseVirtualList`, …) — keep
       the derived work + returned JSX in a `const render = () => …` closure that
       the `<template>` renders via `<component :is="render" v-bind="$attrs" />`
       (the closure is a functional component, so the forwarded `$attrs` land on
       whatever element it returns; since
       `<script setup>` cannot itself *return* a render function), pulling in
       `useSlots()` when the body reads `slots`. The same native multi-word
       `on<Event>` lowercasing (`onDragOver` → `onDragover`) is applied inside the
       closure's JSX/`h()` so `@vitejs/plugin-vue-jsx` binds the real DOM event.
     **Named slots** (`<Slot name="x" />` from `@mission-platform/jsx`) become
     `<slot name="x">` on the template path or `slots.x?.()` on the fallback path,
     and their names are dropped from the runtime `props`; the React emitter
     rewrites the same `<Slot name="x" />` to a `properties.x` render-prop read,
     and never imports the `Slot` marker. When a prop name collides with a JSX
     **attribute name** (`<img src={src}/>` with a `src` prop) or an intrinsic
     **element tag name** (`<caption>` alongside a `caption` prop), only the
     *value* is bound — the attribute/tag name is preserved (so it never becomes
     the invalid `:properties.src` / `properties.src={…}` or a dynamic
     `<properties.caption>`). **Scoped slots:** extra attributes on a `<Slot>`
     (`<Slot name="row" item={item} index={i} />`) become a scope — the Vue
     template emits `<slot name="row" :item="item" :index="i">` (or
     `slots.row?.({ item, index })` on the fallback path) and the React emitter
     calls `properties.row?.({ item, index })`. **Slot presence:** the neutral
     `hasSlot('x')` marker (from `@mission-platform/jsx`) is rewritten to each
     framework's native presence check — the Vue template path emits
     `v-if="$slots.x"`, the Vue render-closure path `!!slots.x` (pulling in
     `useSlots()`), and the React emitter `properties.x != null` — and the
     `hasSlot` import is consumed (never emitted), so a component can gate an
     optional wrapper region on whether a slot is filled. **Passing named slots:** a
     component element whose **children** are marked `slot="name"` routes that
     content into the child's matching slot — the React emitter emits a
     `name={…}` prop, the Vue template path a `<template #name>` block (default
     children in `<template #default>`), and the Vue render-closure path the
     `@vitejs/plugin-vue-jsx` `{{ name: () => … }}` object-children form
     (rewritten *before* the reference rewriter, so setters/state reads inside
     the slot functions are still translated to Vue reactivity); the `slot`
     marker itself is always dropped from the output. **Portals:** the neutral
     `<Teleport to="…">` element (a *framework component*, unlike the consumed
     `Slot` marker) keeps its JSX usage on both targets, but its **import** is
     remapped — Vue resolves `Teleport` straight from the `vue` runtime
     (`import { Teleport } from 'vue'`, added to the SFC's `vue` import) and React
     imports it from the adapter (`import { Teleport } from
     '@mission-platform/jsx/react'`, a `createPortal` wrapper), so each build uses
     its native portal with no neutral runtime. **Transitions:** the neutral
     `<Transition name="…">` and `<TransitionGroup name="…">` elements (more
     *framework components*) keep their JSX usage but their import is remapped —
     Vue resolves them from the `vue` runtime (built-in `<Transition>` /
     `<TransitionGroup>`) and React imports the `@mission-platform/jsx/react`
     CSS-class drivers (single enter/leave for `Transition`; keyed list
     enter/leave/move for `TransitionGroup`). **Dynamic components:** a
     `<Dynamic is={X} …>` marker is rewritten to an `h(X, …)` call (with
     `class`→`className` aliasing on React), which React's classic-`h` transform
     compiles to `createElement(X, …)` and the Vue emitter renders as
     `<component :is="X">`; like `Slot`, the `Dynamic` marker import is consumed.
     Hyphenated attributes (`aria-current`, `data-id`) are emitted as quoted
     string-literal prop keys (valid JS), and `<Slot>` children are unwrapped to
     bare `h()` arguments, so a `<Dynamic>` may carry slotted children
     (`<Dynamic is={tag}><Slot/></Dynamic>`).
     **Context:** the `createContext`/`useContext` primitives map to each
     framework's native provide/inject — on React they *are* React's own (their
     import falls through to `react`, so `<Ctx.Provider value>` is a native
     provider), while on Vue the import is remapped to
     `@mission-platform/jsx/vue` (a `provide`/`inject`-backed implementation) and
     a `const x = useContext(ctx)` is kept a **synchronous setup const** (never
     lifted to a `computed`, so `inject()` runs in setup). **Recursion:** a
     component that references **itself** as a JSX tag compiles natively — the
     React self-reference is an ordinary in-scope function, and the Vue
     render-closure resolves it by name (`resolveComponent('<name>')`, backed by
     the SFC's `defineOptions({ name })`).
2. **Stage 2 — native compile.** The generated source tree is compiled by the
   framework's *own* toolchain — the classic-`h` React JSX transform (configured
   by `reactJsxPlugin`) or `@vitejs/plugin-vue` (+ `@vitejs/plugin-vue-jsx`).

Adding another target framework is just another emitter folder in
`src/generators/` — each target lives in its own directory with an `index.ts`
barrel re-exporting its public emitter and the implementation split across
focused files: `react/` (`aliases.ts`, `imports.ts`, `emit-module.ts`), `vue/`
(`shared.ts`, `scope.ts`, `effects.ts`, `body.ts`, `template.ts`, `imports.ts`,
`styles.ts`, `emit-module.ts`), and `storyblok/` (`types.ts`, `names.ts`, `classify.ts`,
`analyze.ts`, `wrappers.ts`) — with no new runtime and no changes to the neutral
source. The shared parsing/discovery helpers live in `src/compiler/` (`ast.ts`,
`compile.ts`, `discover.ts`).

## Storyblok target

The same neutral source also projects onto **Storyblok**, deriving two artefacts
per component from its props *contract* (it never rewrites the body):

1. **The blok configuration** — a Storyblok *component object* (the shape the
   Management API's create endpoint and `storyblok push-components` consume).
   The props interface maps onto a Storyblok `schema`: string-literal unions
   (incl. those declared as local `type` aliases) → `option` fields with
   self-sourced `options`; `boolean`/`number`/`string` → the matching primitive
   field; `string | number` (and other mixed unions) → free `text`; callback
   props are **dropped** (not authorable); the default slot (`children`) and
   `MpChild` named-slot props → nestable `bloks` fields. Prop JSDoc becomes the
   field `description` and the `properties.x ?? <literal>` / `{ x = <literal> }`
   defaults become `default_value`. Names are derived from the public name
   (`InView` → technical `in_view`, display `In View`).
2. **A framework blok wrapper** — a thin React `.tsx` / Vue `.vue` component
   that takes Storyblok's `blok` prop, forwards each schema field to the
   matching prop of the **built** framework component (imported from the
   package's `./react` / `./vue` subpath), tags it editable
   (`storyblokEditable(blok)` / `v-editable="blok"`), and renders each `bloks`
   field through `@storyblok/{react,vue}`'s `StoryblokComponent`. The wrapper's
   `blok` prop is **precisely typed** — `SbBlokData & { … }` with one member per
   schema field (`option` → string-literal union, `text` → `string`, `number`,
   `boolean`, `bloks` → `SbBlokData[]`; non-optional props stay required), not an
   open `Record<string, unknown>`. {@link emitBlokDataType} builds that type from
   the same analysis, and a field-less component degrades to bare `SbBlokData`.

`generateStoryblokBloks` writes, per component, `<folder>.json` (the
`{ "component": … }` create shape) and `<folder>.{tsx,vue}` (the wrapper), plus
the aggregate `components.json` (the `{ "components": [ … ] }` push shape), a
wrapper entry barrel re-exporting each `<Name>Blok`, and the entry's synthesised,
precisely typed `index.d.ts` (the barrel is handed to Vite's `lib.entry`,
compiled natively by Stage 2 like the framework sources).

### Stylesheets & framework-agnostic utilities

- **Component-owned stylesheets.** Relative CSS / CSS-Module imports
  (`import styles from './x.module.scss'` or a bare side-effect import) let a
  neutral component own and ship its own CSS on every framework, scoped by each
  framework's idiomatic mechanism:
  - **React** keeps the **CSS Module** — the import is carried verbatim (the
    stylesheet copied next to the emitted module and re-pointed at the flat
    copy) and the hashed `styles[...]` class names are preserved.
  - **Vue** inlines a CSS-Module default import (`import styles …`) as a
    **non-scoped** `<style lang="scss">` block in the generated SFC (the
    `@layer mp.components` wrapper is preserved), so the Vue build uses **plain**
    (BEM) class names; the rewriter collapses every `styles['x']` /
    `` styles[`x`] `` read — including computed object keys
    (`{ [styles['x--mod']]: cond }`) — to its literal class name. The block is
    intentionally **not** `scoped`: the render-closure-fallback SFCs render via a
    `render` closure delegated from the `<template>` (`<component :is="render" />`)
    and Vue only applies a `<style scoped>` `data-v-` attribute to that render
    output's **root** vnode, so nested elements would be left unstyled (and a
    single, consistent strategy keeps the template and fallback paths
    interchangeable);
    the unique BEM names + `@layer mp.components` provide the namespacing instead
    (matching the original `@mission-platform/components` SFCs). Bare side-effect
    CSS imports are still carried verbatim.
- **Framework-agnostic runtime values.** Neutral value imports that behave
  identically on every target — currently `classNames` — are *not* translated
  like `h`/the hooks; their `import { classNames } from '@mission-platform/jsx'`
  is preserved verbatim in both the React and Vue output.
- **The `classNames={…}` attribute.** The platform-owned class attribute (the
  neutral counterpart of `className`/`class`, the author never imports the
  helper) is consumed by the compiler: on **React** an **array** value collapses
  to a `className={classNames(…)}` string call (the variadic helper) — and the
  emitter re-injects the neutral `classNames` import for it — while any other
  value is a single class string passed straight through as `className`; on
  **Vue** it maps onto the native `class` binding (`:class="[…]"`), which already
  understands the array/object forms, so no helper is needed. The plain `class`
  attribute (reserved for static strings) keeps its existing `class`→`className`
  (React) / `class` (Vue) handling.
- **External (bare-package) imports.** Any other bare-package import (e.g.
  `@mission-platform/forms-core`, `luxon`) is carried **verbatim** into the
  generated source so values it provides — used by the body, carried-over
  helpers, or prop defaults — resolve at runtime. The one exception is the
  write-once icon library `@mission-platform/icons`, which publishes only its
  per-framework builds: its import is **remapped** to `@mission-platform/icons/vue`
  on the Vue target and `@mission-platform/icons/react` on the React target
  (the Vue path in `readExternalImports`, the React path in the React emitter's
  import pass), so a neutral `<IconChevron …/>` resolves to the native framework
  icon while its JSX usage is left intact — the same neutral-to-framework remap
  pattern as `Teleport`/`Transition`.
- **Shared helper modules.** A neutral component may import a sibling **helper
  module** (a plain `.ts`/`.tsx` next to the component folders, e.g. a ported
  store) with an ordinary relative import. `generateFrameworkSources` passes the
  set of discovered component folders to the compiler so the Vue emitter can tell
  a sibling **component** (rendered as `import X from './x.vue'`) apart from a
  helper (kept as a named `import { … } from './x'`), and copies each referenced
  helper file verbatim into the flat generated tree (re-pointing the import) on
  both targets. Helpers must be framework-agnostic (no neutral/JSX imports).
- **Per-component CSS in library builds.** With `build.lib` + `cssCodeSplit`,
  Vite extracts one CSS asset per component chunk but does **not** inject the
  matching `import './x.css'` into the JS chunk; `jsxComponentsCssImportPlugin`
  (running `enforce: 'post'`, so Vite has already populated `importedCss`)
  restores that link so importing a single component pulls in exactly its own
  stylesheet (and the rest of the library — styles included — tree-shakes).

## Install

Consumed inside the monorepo as a workspace dependency:

```jsonc
// packages/<consumer>/package.json
{
  "devDependencies": {
    "@mission-platform/vite-plugin-jsx": "workspace:*"
  }
}
```

`vite`, `react`/`react-dom`, and `vue` are optional peer dependencies — only the
framework you target needs to be present. `typescript` is a runtime dependency
(the Stage-1 compiler uses its compiler API).

## Usage

Run one build per target framework. Stage 1 generates the per-framework source
tree; Stage 2 compiles it with the framework's plugins.

```ts
// vite.config.ts (React target)
import { generateFrameworkSources, jsxComponentsEntryDtsPlugin, reactJsxPlugin } from '@mission-platform/vite-plugin-jsx';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

const componentsModule = '/abs/path/to/src/components/index.ts';
const entry = generateFrameworkSources({ framework: 'react', componentsModule, outDir: '/abs/cache/react' });

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [reactJsxPlugin(), jsxComponentsEntryDtsPlugin({ framework: 'react', componentsModule, declarationFileName: 'react' })],
  build: { lib: { entry, fileName: 'react', formats: ['es'] } },
});
```

```ts
// vite.config.ts (Vue target)
import { generateFrameworkSources, jsxComponentsEntryDtsPlugin } from '@mission-platform/vite-plugin-jsx';
import vue from '@vitejs/plugin-vue';
import vueJsx from '@vitejs/plugin-vue-jsx';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

const componentsModule = '/abs/path/to/src/components/index.ts';
const entry = generateFrameworkSources({ framework: 'vue', componentsModule, outDir: '/abs/cache/vue' });

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [vue(), vueJsx(), jsxComponentsEntryDtsPlugin({ framework: 'vue', componentsModule, declarationFileName: 'vue' })],
  build: { lib: { entry, fileName: 'vue', formats: ['es'] } },
});
```

The Storyblok target additionally emits the blok configuration JSON and a
framework blok wrapper. Compile the returned wrapper entry with the same Stage-2
plugins as the matching framework:

```ts
// vite.config.ts (Storyblok wrappers for the Vue build)
import { generateStoryblokBloks } from '@mission-platform/vite-plugin-jsx';
import vue from '@vitejs/plugin-vue';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

const componentsModule = '/abs/path/to/src/components/index.ts';
const entry = generateStoryblokBloks({
  framework: 'vue',
  componentsModule,
  outDir: '/abs/cache/storyblok-vue', // contains <name>.json, <name>.vue, components.json
  componentsImport: '@mission-platform/components/vue',
});

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [vue()],
  build: { lib: { entry, fileName: 'storyblok', formats: ['es'] } },
});
```

## API

### `generateFrameworkSources(options): string` (Stage 1)

Reads the neutral components barrel, compiles each component to the target
framework, writes the generated source tree + a public entry into `outDir`, and
returns the entry path (use it as the Vite `lib.entry`).

- `options.framework: 'react' | 'vue'` — required target framework.
- `options.componentsModule: string` — absolute path of the neutral barrel
  (`src/components/index.ts`). Components are resolved by convention at
  `<dir>/<name>/<name>.tsx`.
- `options.outDir: string` — absolute path the generated tree is written to
  (cleaned on each run). Use a build-cache directory.
- `options.stripPrefix?: string` — prefix removed from each neutral name to form
  its public name. Defaults to `Base` (so `BaseBadge` ships as `Badge`).

The generated entry re-exports each component under **both** its public name
(`Badge`) **and** its original neutral `stripPrefix`-prefixed name (`BaseBadge`)
as aliases of the same component, so consumers can import under either
convention. It also re-exports **every type** each component ships alongside it
(variants, option shapes, props interfaces, scoped-slot scopes, …) from the
neutral declarations.

### `generateStoryblokBloks(options): string`

Projects the neutral barrel onto Storyblok: writes each component's blok
configuration JSON + a framework blok wrapper into `outDir`, plus the aggregate
`components.json`, the wrapper entry barrel (whose path it returns, for use as
the Vite `lib.entry`), and the entry's synthesised, precisely typed `index.d.ts`
(each `<Name>Blok` typed with a `SbBlokData & { … }` `blok` prop).

- `options.framework: 'react' | 'vue'` — which wrapper to emit (`.tsx` / `.vue`).
- `options.componentsModule: string` — absolute path of the neutral barrel.
- `options.outDir: string` — absolute output directory (cleaned on each run).
- `options.componentsImport: string` — specifier the wrappers import the **built**
  components from (e.g. `@mission-platform/components/vue`).
- `options.stripPrefix?: string` — prefix removed from each neutral name (default
  `Base`).

### `emitStoryblokComponent(sourceFile, names)` / `analyzeStoryblokComponent(...)` / `emitStoryblokBlokWrapper(analyzed, publicName, options)` / `emitBlokDataType(analyzed)`

The pure Storyblok transforms of a single parsed module (useful for testing):
the component object, the component object plus per-field metadata, the framework
wrapper source, and the wrapper's precise `blok` prop type (`SbBlokData & { … }`,
one member per schema field; bare `SbBlokData` when field-less), respectively.

### `compileComponentModule(source, options): { code, lang }`

The pure Stage-1 transform of a single module (useful for testing). Returns the
emitted source and its extension (`tsx` for React, `vue` for Vue).

### `reactJsxPlugin(): Plugin` (Stage 2, React)

A Vite plugin that sets `esbuild.jsxFactory = 'h'` / `jsxFragment = 'Fragment'`
for the generated React sources. The Vue target needs no esbuild JSX config — it
uses `@vitejs/plugin-vue` + `@vitejs/plugin-vue-jsx` instead.

### `jsxComponentsEntryDtsPlugin({ framework, componentsModule, declarationFileName, … }): Plugin`

Synthesises the `<declarationFileName>.d.ts` for the generated entry (typing each
export as `FunctionComponent` / `DefineComponent<…Properties>` under **both** its
public and neutral `Base*` name), since the generated entry is not a source file
`tsc` emits types for. Props types — and every other public type each component
re-exports (variants, scoped-slot scopes, …) — are imported/re-exported from the
neutral components' own emitted declarations (`declarationModule`, default
`./components`).

### `jsxComponentsCssImportPlugin(): Plugin`

For a `build.lib` + `cssCodeSplit` build (per-component CSS chunks), prepends a
side-effect `import './x.css'` to every JS chunk for each CSS file Vite
associated with it (`chunk.viteMetadata.importedCss`), so each component loads
its own stylesheet without a combined CSS export. It runs with `enforce: 'post'`
so its `generateBundle` hook fires **after** Vite has populated `importedCss` —
without that, the metadata is still empty (e.g. for Vue's extracted `<style>`
assets under `preserveModules`) and the per-component CSS is left orphaned.

## Relationship to `@mission-platform/jsx`

`@mission-platform/jsx` owns the neutral primitives (`h`, `Fragment`,
`MpElement`, `MpProperties`, the React-style hooks, …) and the **runtime**
`./react` / `./vue` adapters (`toReactComponent` / `toVueComponent`) used for
ad-hoc/SSR rendering. This plugin is the **build-time** path: it compiles the
neutral source straight to each framework so the shipped artifact is an ordinary
React or Vue component (see `@mission-platform/components`).

## Helper re-exports through the generated entry

Besides the components, the entry generator also forwards a barrel's
**helper-module** re-exports — any `export { … } from './<helper>'` whose module
is not a component folder (e.g. `export { useToast, showToast, … } from
'./toast-store'`). `discoverHelperExports` collects their value + type names and
`generateEntry` / `generateEntryDeclaration` emit matching re-exports in the
generated `./react` / `./vue` entry (re-pointing to the helper file copied into
the flat per-framework tree) and its synthesised `.d.ts` (pointing at the
`tsc`-emitted `../components/<helper>` declaration). This lets a write-once
package expose shared framework-agnostic APIs alongside its components so each
framework's consumers drive the same per-framework singleton the components use.
PascalCase component re-exports are never treated as helpers, and a helper line
never produces a phantom component.
